text: The US, UK and EU governments attribute this group to Russian military intelligence (GRU Unit 74455). It is linked to the 2015 and 2016 power grid attacks in Ukraine, the 2017 NotPetya attack and the 2018 Winter Olympics attack. Its work is destructive: wipers and attacks on industrial control systems.

The US, UK and other governments have attributed APT29 to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR). In April 2021 the US and UK attributed the 2020 SolarWinds Orion compromise to the SVR, and MITRE says the group has operated since at least 2008.

APT-C-60 is the name JPCERT/CC uses for a threat group it says likely carried out spear-phishing attacks on organizations in Japan from August 2024, using fake job-applicant emails and a backdoor called SpyGlace. No government or MITRE source opened for this page says who is behind it.

The US FBI (July 2026) describes TeamPCP as a cyber criminal group behind large-scale software supply chain compromises of widely used developer and security tools. Australian and US authorities announced arrests and an indictment linked to the group in August 2026, and MITRE ATT&CK describes it as active since at least September 2025.

MITRE describes APT41 as a Chinese state-sponsored espionage group, as researchers have assessed it, that also runs financially motivated operations. The US Department of Justice charged five Chinese nationals in 2019 and 2020 and said the hacking reached more than 100 victims.

The US Treasury, FBI and Department of Justice attributed APT39, also called Chafer, to Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS), working through the front company Rana Intelligence Computing Company, in September 2020. The US sanctioned the company and 45 people.

APT38 is a North Korean state-sponsored group focused on financial theft, attributed by MITRE ATT&CK to North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau. MITRE lists banks, cryptocurrency exchanges and SWIFT system endpoints among its targets. The US Department of Justice named APT38 in November 2025 forfeiture cases over four 2023 cryptocurrency heists.

MITRE ATT&CK describes APT32 (OceanLotus) as a suspected Vietnam-based threat group active since at least 2014 that targets governments, dissidents, journalists and companies, mainly in Southeast Asia. CERT-EU calls it Vietnam-linked, but no government indictment or sanction names it. The latest dated activity in these sources is January 2025.

The US, UK, EU and other governments attribute APT28 to Russia's military intelligence service, the GRU, specifically its 85th Main Special Service Center (military unit 26165). MITRE says the group has been active since at least 2004, and government advisories describe espionage against governments, militaries, political parties, media and logistics firms.

Lazarus Group is the name used by MITRE, the US Treasury and the US Department of Justice for North Korean hacking units. They say these units work for the Reconnaissance General Bureau. The US charged three RGB members in 2020 and 2021 with attempts to steal or extort more than $1.3 billion. The FBI attributed the 2025 Bybit theft to North Korean actors it tracks as TraderTraitor.

Attributed by MITRE ATT&CK and by the US Department of Justice (5 March 2025) to a Chinese group, also called Threat Group-3390 and Emissary Panda, that targets governments and companies. The Justice Department charged two men it calls APT27 actors, alleging profit-driven hacking from 2013 to 2024.

MITRE ATT&CK, the FBI, CISA, NCSC-UK and the US Treasury attribute this group to Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). It is described as running cyber espionage against telecommunications, defense, local government and oil and gas organizations. The 2022 joint advisory says it gets in by spearphishing and known software flaws. It says the group shares access with other actors.

Attributed by the US and UK governments (19 July 2021) to the Chinese state, and charged by the US Department of Justice (8 July 2025) as directed by officers of China's Ministry of State Security, HAFNIUM is the name of the actor behind the campaign that exploited Microsoft Exchange Server flaws in early 2021. MITRE describes it as a likely state-sponsored espionage group that targets US universities, law firms, defense contractors and research bodies.

Attributed by MITRE ATT&CK to PLA Unit 61398 in China, APT1 is the subject of a US indictment of 19 May 2014 charging five Unit 61398 officers with hacking six US organizations. The Department of Justice alleges the aim was commercial gain for China's state-owned firms.

Singapore's cyber agency (CSA) calls UNC3886 a state-sponsored group without naming a state, and MITRE ATT&CK describes it as China-nexus, in entries dated 2025 and 2026. The group is reported to break into firewalls, routers and virtualization hosts for espionage, and CSA says it targeted all four major Singapore telecom operators.

Scattered Spider is described by MITRE ATT&CK and by the FBI, CISA and partner agencies as a cybercriminal group that targets large companies and their IT help desks, mainly by tricking staff into resetting passwords and MFA. The UK National Crime Agency said on 16 July 2026 that its action against two leading members effectively halted the group, while others may reuse the name.

MITRE ATT&CK describes APT37, also called ScarCruft, as a North Korean state-sponsored cyber espionage group that has been active since at least 2012. It targets South Korea first, using spearphishing emails with Hangul (HWP) attachments, compromised websites and cloud services for control. No government advisory opened names the group itself.

The UK, US, Australian, Canadian and New Zealand governments attribute this group to Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) Center 18. It is linked to long phishing campaigns against politicians, researchers, journalists and government staff in the UK, US and other NATO countries. It steals email logins and reads the victims' mail.

The US Cyber Safety Review Board describes Lapsus$ as a loosely organized, extortion-focused criminal group based mainly in the United Kingdom and Brazil, and UK and Brazilian police have made arrests in cases linked to it. It tricked staff, used stolen logins, and stole or deleted company data.

Wizard Spider is a Russia-based criminal group behind the Trickbot malware, attributed by the US Department of Justice and Treasury, the UK government and Germany's BKA. Its work is stealing money and data and installing ransomware such as Ryuk and Conti. In 2023 the US charged nine members and the US and UK sanctioned 18 people.

entity_name: Nefilim Ransomware: Profile, Tactics and the Stryzhak Case
text:
Nefilim was a ransomware-as-a-service operation that stole data, encrypted networks and threatened to publish what it took. The US Department of Justice says its administrators gave affiliates access in return for a percentage of ransom payments; affiliate Artem Stryzhak agreed to pay 20%. On 27 October 2026 a US court sentenced him to 70 months in prison.

Modelo: Ransomware as a service with double extortion; affiliate Stryzhak agreed to pay the administrators 20% of ransom proceeds (per the US Department of Justice)

Extorsão: Double extortion. The DOJ says Nefilim ransom notes typically threatened that, unless the victim came to an agreement, the stolen data would be published on public "Corporate Leaks" websites kept by the Nefilim administrators. The DOJ says victims who paid received a decryption key. In its plea release it adds that a unique ransomware file, with its own key and ransom note, was made for each victim.

Conti was a ransomware as a service operation first observed in December 2019, per MITRE ATT&CK. A joint advisory (AA21-265A) from CISA, the FBI and the NSA, first published September 22, 2021, says it hit U.S. and international organizations in more than 400 attacks at first and above 1,000 by March 2022. The U.S. Department of Justice says the conspiracy ran until about June 2022.

Modelo: Ransomware as a service, with a wage model per CISA

Extorsão: Double extortion, per CISA: files are stolen and servers and workstations are encrypted. The victim is told to pay for the release of the data and is threatened with public release if it does not. Rewards for Justice says the stolen data is sold or published on a leak site if the ransom is not paid, and that some demands reached 25 million US dollars.

Rhysida is a ransomware operation that CISA, the FBI and the MS-ISAC say has mainly been deployed against education, healthcare, manufacturing, IT and government organizations since May 2023. Open source reporting describes it as a ransomware-as-a-service model where any ransom is split with associates. Rhysida uses double extortion: victims pay to decrypt files and pay again to stop stolen data being published.

Modelo: Ransomware as a service (profit-sharing with associates)

Extorsão: Double extortion. Victims are told to pay in Bitcoin both to decrypt files and to stop stolen data being published. A PDF ransom note points to a Tor portal.

RansomHub is a ransomware as a service operation, formerly known as Cyclops and Knight, according to a joint advisory (AA24-242A) from the FBI, CISA, MS-ISAC and HHS released on August 29, 2024. The advisory says it had encrypted and stolen data from at least 210 victims since its start in February 2024. Ransomware as a service means the core team rents its malware to partner criminals, called affiliates.

Modelo: Ransomware as a service

Extorsão: Double extortion, per the advisory: affiliates encrypt systems and steal data. The ransom note gives a client ID and a unique Tor address (a hidden site reached with the Tor browser) rather than a price. It typically allows between three and 90 days, depending on the affiliate, before data is published on the RansomHub leak site.

KillSec is a ransomware and data extortion group that Europol says has been active since around 2024. On 30 September 2026 law enforcement took control of its leak site, securing at least 110 terabytes of data, in an operation led by German authorities.

Modelo: Data theft and extortion by a group whose suspected members held administrator, developer, negotiator and affiliate roles (attributed by Europol)

Extorsão: Data theft and threats, per Europol: victims were named on the group's dark web leak site and threatened with publication of their data unless they paid. Where a victim did not pay, the stolen files could be made available for free download. In some cases the group obtained substantial ransom payments.

Cobalt Strike is a commercial remote access tool sold for adversary simulation, which means security teams use it to test their own networks. CISA, the FBI and the NCSC also report attackers using it after a break-in to control machines, move across the network and take data. Its main payload is called Beacon.

Impacket is a free, open source set of Python modules for working with network protocols. It includes tools for running commands on remote machines, dumping Windows credentials, working with Kerberos tickets, sniffing traffic and relaying logins. Defenders see it mostly because attackers, including state actors and ransomware groups named in CISA advisories, use it once they are inside a network.

NotPetya is destructive malware that looks like ransomware. MITRE says the attackers never intended the encrypted data to be recoverable, so it is better thought of as a wiper. It spread across networks from 27 June 2017 and has been attributed by the UK, the US and others to the Russian military.

CROSSROAD is the name Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant give to a downloader used in a 2026 tampering of AOMEI Backupper updates. It ran on a computer when the backup program fetched a tampered update, then set up a backdoor that they name SHINYROAD.

Snake, also called Uroburos, is a cyber espionage implant written in C, with versions for Windows, Linux and macOS. US and allied agencies attribute it to a unit in Center 16 of Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB), which they say used it for long-term intelligence collection. It hides on the host, and its infected machines form a covert peer-to-peer network that relays stolen data.
